titleEn: God is the judge: one He lowers, one He lifts
progression: | Em Em | C C | D D | Em Em |
intro: Eleven verses that change speaker three times without announcing it: a congregation gives thanks, God answers in the first person, and a single voice turns to warn the arrogant. Asaph's name is on the heading, as it is on Psalm 50 and on the run from 73 to 83. The word to follow is horn, which appears four times and means the raised head of an animal, so power that can be seen from a distance. Almost everything in the psalm is either being lifted or being brought down. In the thirty-day reading cycle it falls on the fourteenth day.

stichs.en: For the leader, to the tune Do Not Destroy.
A psalm of Asaph, a song.

verses.summary: The heading names a melody, and the two words that name it are a prohibition. The same two words come back inside the psalm, aimed at people rather than at a tune.

stichs.en: We have given thanks to You, God, we have given thanks,
and Your name is near;
they recount Your wonders.

verses.summary: Thanks are given twice before any reason is stated. The reason, when it comes, is nearness, and in this psalm a near name means a judge already in the room.

stichs.en: When I take the appointed time,
I Myself will judge with fairness.

verses.summary: God takes over the sentence with no introduction. The claim is about timing rather than power: the judge is not absent, He is holding a date.

stichs.en: The earth and all who live on it are dissolving;
I Myself have set her pillars firm. Selah.

verses.summary: Both halves are stated as already true: the ground is giving way and the supports are already fixed. That is why the verse can end in Selah instead of a request.

stichs.en: I said to the boastful, Do not boast,
and to the wicked, Do not raise a horn.

verses.summary: The voice shifts again, to a human speaker addressing two groups. The warning turns the boasters' own root back on them as a verb.

stichs.en: Do not raise your horn up high;
you speak with an arrogant neck.

verses.summary: The horn goes up and the neck stiffens. Arrogance is described entirely as posture, and the speech is presented as coming out of the posture.

stichs.en: For not from the east and not from the west,
and not from the wilderness of mountains.

verses.summary: Three directions are ruled out and the fourth, upward, is left unsaid. Promotion does not travel along a compass bearing.

stichs.en: For God is judge:
this one He brings low, and this one He raises.

verses.summary: The whole argument in seven words, with the two verbs side by side and one subject doing both. Nothing is said about who deserves which.

stichs.en: For there is a cup in the LORD's hand,
foaming wine, full of mixed spices,
and He pours from it;
surely all the wicked of the earth will drain its dregs and drink.

verses.summary: The longest verse and the only image the psalm develops at length: a cup poured out, and the sediment left for whoever drinks last. The reckoning is served rather than announced.

stichs.en: But as for me, I will declare for ever,
I will sing to the God of Jacob.

verses.summary: The singer separates himself with the same two-word construction Psalm 71 uses at its own hinge, and commits to the same pair of verbs: declare and sing.

stichs.en: And all the horns of the wicked I will cut off;
the horns of the righteous will be lifted high.

verses.summary: The horns come back, cut off in one clause and raised in the next. Who is speaking here is not marked in the Hebrew, and the verse is read both ways.

pardes.body: A courtroom psalm with no trial scene in it, only the announcement that a date has been set. The congregation speaks in verse 2, God speaks in verses 3 and 4, a human voice warns the arrogant from verse 5, and by verse 11 it is no longer marked who is speaking at all. The physical spine is the horn, the raised head of a bull or a ram and the standard image for visible power: it is forbidden at {{5.7}} and {{6.3}}, cut off at {{11.1}}, and lifted at {{11.5}}. Around it the verb for raising keeps returning, in the warning at {{6.1}}, in the verdict at {{8.6}}, and in the last line at {{11.4}}. The wicked raise their own horn; the righteous have theirs raised for them.

The heading is a tune name, Do Not Destroy, which also heads Psalms 57, 58 and 59, and its two words {{1.1}} and {{1.2}} are exactly the form the psalm uses later for its own prohibitions at {{5.2}} and {{6.0}}. The real crux is {{7.6}}. The same consonants can be read as the plural noun mountains, giving the wilderness of mountains as a fourth place that promotion does not come from, or as a form of the verb to lift, which is how the JPS translation takes it when it renders the line as nor yet from the wilderness cometh lifting up. Both readings are current and the Hebrew does not settle it. Note that on the second reading the verse ends on the psalm's key verb, which would make the crux the hinge. {{4.7}} is another unsettled word: Selah is a performance direction whose meaning is not known.

The cup at {{9.1}} is not this psalm's invention. It is the cup of wrath the prophets pass around, poured out in Isaiah 51 and handed to the nations in Jeremiah 25, and its logic is that judgement is a drink rather than a blow: everyone gets a share, and the last share is the sediment. Read together with {{3.2}}, the appointed time, the psalm becomes an answer to the oldest complaint in the book, that the wicked prosper. The answer offered is not that they do not prosper but that the matter is scheduled, and that a docket held by a judge who has set the pillars of the earth is not the same thing as a case that has been dropped.

Verse 4 sets two states of the world against each other in one line: at {{4.0}} the earth and everything on it are melting, and at {{4.5}} the pillars are already fixed. The world is dissolving and standing at the same time, and it holds because of an act described in the first person singular. Read the last word of the psalm back into that image and the pillar acquires a name: {{11.6}} is a singular, the righteous one, and Proverbs 10 calls the righteous the foundation of the world. What is lifted at the end is then not a reward handed to a person but the load-bearing member of the structure being put back in place.
